The term "op-ed" is short for "opposite the editorial page."

To understand this, you first need to picture a traditional printed newspaper. Inside a newspaper, there is a dedicated page called the editorial page. This is where the newspaper's own editors and editorial board publish their official opinions — the stance of the newspaper itself on current issues.

Now, directly across from that page — the page physically facing it — is what newspapers call the op-ed page. Whatever gets published on that facing page is called an op-ed piece.

So "op-ed" is simply a location reference — it describes where on the newspaper the article appeared. But over time, the term grew to mean something much richer than just a physical position on a page.

An op-ed piece is an opinion article written by someone who does not work for the newspaper — an outsider, a guest voice. This person writes about a current event, a social issue, a political matter, a scientific topic, or any subject they feel strongly and knowledgeably about. Crucially, they don't just report on it — they argue a point of view about it.

Think of it this way: a news reporter tells you what happened. An op-ed writer tells you what they think it means, why it matters, and what should be done about it.

The concept is generally traced back to Herbert Bayard Swope, an editor at the New York World newspaper, who introduced the idea in 1921. He noticed that the page facing the editorial page was mostly wasted space and decided to fill it with outside voices and opinions.

However, the term "op-ed" and the modern format we recognize today were truly popularized by The New York Times, which launched a formal, dedicated op-ed page in September 1970. The goal was to open up a space in a major newspaper for voices beyond the editorial staff — intellectuals, experts, activists, political figures, and engaged citizens — to speak directly to the public. It was a revolutionary idea in journalism at the time and quickly became standard practice worldwide.

Almost anyone can write an op-ed, provided they have something meaningful to say and can say it well. In practice, op-ed writers typically fall into one of these categories:

Experts and professionals — A doctor writing about a public health crisis. An economist arguing against a tax policy. A climate scientist warning about a new environmental report.

Politicians and public officials — A senator defending a new bill. A former president reflecting on a foreign policy decision.

Academics and researchers — A professor explaining why a popular belief is factually wrong. A historian drawing a parallel between today's events and the past.

Activists and advocates — Someone pushing for criminal justice reform, writing a passionate, evidence-backed argument for change.

Business leaders — A CEO making the case for or against new regulation.

Ordinary citizens with relevant, first-hand experience — A veteran writing about the realities of war. A formerly incarcerated person writing about prison conditions.

The common thread is this: the writer has a specific point of view, some form of authority or lived experience to back it up, and something they want the public to think about or act on.
The Core Characteristics of an Op-Ed

These are the defining features that make an op-ed what it is:

1. It is opinion, not neutral reporting.
An op-ed takes a clear, definite side. The writer believes something and wants you to consider believing it too. This is completely intentional and transparent — readers know they are reading opinion, not objective news.

2. It is written by an outside contributor.
This is critical. The writer is not a staff journalist of the publication. They are a guest voice.

3. It is backed by reasoning and evidence.
A good op-ed is not just a rant or an emotional outburst. It supports its argument with facts, data, examples, expert knowledge, or compelling personal experience. The goal is to persuade through logic, not just emotion.

4. It addresses a timely, relevant issue.
Op-eds are almost always triggered by something happening in the world right now — a new law, a recent event, a growing social debate. They connect the writer's viewpoint to something the public is already paying attention to.

5. It has a clear argument and a call to action.
A strong op-ed doesn't meander. It states a clear thesis, builds a case, and often ends by urging readers, policymakers, or society to do something specific.

While there's no single rigid formula, most op-eds follow a recognizable shape:

  • A hook — An opening line or short paragraph that grabs your attention immediately. This might be a surprising statistic, a vivid personal story, a bold claim, or a provocative question.
  • The thesis — A clear statement of what the writer believes and what they are arguing.
  • The body — The argument, built with evidence, examples, expert citations, and reasoning. This is where the writer makes their case.
  • Acknowledgment of the other side (optional but effective) — Strong op-eds sometimes briefly address the opposing viewpoint and explain why it falls short.
  • The conclusion / call to action — A powerful closing that reinforces the main point and often urges the reader or decision-makers to take a specific action or adopt a new way of thinking.

A typical op-ed runs between 600 and 900 words, though this varies by publication.
How an Op-Ed Differs from Similar Things

This is where many people get confused, so let's be precise:

Op-ed vs. News Article
A news article is supposed to be objective and factual — it reports what happened without telling you what to think about it. An op-ed is openly subjective — it tells you exactly what the writer thinks, and why.

Op-ed vs. Editorial
This is the most important distinction. An editorial is also an opinion piece, but it is written by the newspaper's own editorial board and represents the official position of the publication itself. An op-ed, by contrast, is written by an outsider and represents only that individual's views — not the publication's. A newspaper can publish an op-ed it profoundly disagrees with, simply because it values the contribution to public debate.

Op-ed vs. Column
A column is a recurring opinion piece written by a regular, contracted writer — someone like a well-known journalist or commentator who has a dedicated slot in the publication every week. An op-ed is usually a one-time submission from a guest writer.

Op-ed vs. Letter to the Editor
A letter to the editor is a short, informal message from a reader responding to something the newspaper published. It's usually just a few sentences or a short paragraph. An op-ed is a full-length, carefully constructed argument — much longer, more formal, and more substantive.

Op-eds serve a vital function in a democratic society. They:

  • Amplify expert voices on issues where public understanding is lacking.
  • Hold power accountable by giving outsiders a platform to challenge government, corporations, or dominant narratives.
  • Enrich public debate by introducing perspectives that the newspaper's own staff might not have.
  • Drive policy change — many famous op-eds have directly influenced legislation, public opinion, or major decisions.
  • Give citizens a voice — they democratize the media by allowing people outside the traditional press to participate in national conversations.

Today, the word "op-ed" has expanded beyond its original physical meaning. Even though most news is now consumed online (where there is no literal "page opposite the editorial page"), the term is still widely used to describe any opinion article by an outside contributor published in a credible outlet. Some publications now prefer the terms "opinion piece," "commentary," "perspective," or "guest essay" — but they all refer to essentially the same thing as an op-ed.

If you ever need to explain it quickly: An op-ed piece is a clearly opinionated article written by an outside expert or engaged citizen — not the newspaper's own staff — that argues a specific point of view on a current issue, with the goal of persuading readers and contributing to public debate.
